source_text:
Ἀλλὰ χάρις τῷ θεῷ: κατὰ πάντων γὰρ οὐκ ἴσχυσεν. ὁ γὰρ γενναιότατος Γερμανικὸς ἐπερρώννυεν αὐτῶν τὴν δειλίαν διὰ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ ὑπομονῆς: ὃς καὶ ἐπισήμως ἐθηριομάχησεν. βουλομένου γὰρ τοῦ ἀνθυπάτου πείθειν αὐτὸν καὶ λέγοντος, τὴν ἡλικίαν αὐτοῦ κατοικτεῖραι, ἑαυτῷ ἐπεσπάσατο τὸ θηρίον προσβιασάμενος, τάχιον τοῦ ἀδίκου καὶ ἀνόμου βίου αὐτῶν ἀπαλλαγῆναι βουλόμενος.
ἐκ τούτου οὖν πᾶν τὸ πλῆθος, θαυμάσαν τὴν γενναιότητα τοῦ θεοφιλοῦς καὶ θεοσεβοῦς γένους τῶν Χριστιανῶν, ἐπεβόησεν: Αἶρε τοὺς ἀθέους: ζητείσθω Πολύκαρπος.
thought_title: Germanicus's courage and the crowd's cry for Polycarp
orientation: The Smyrnaean church is recounting the martyrs' endurance, and now singles out Germanicus, whose bravery in the arena prompts the crowd to demand Polycarp.
pass_a_gloss: But thanks be to God: for against all he did not prevail. For the most noble Germanicus was emboldening them against their cowardice through the endurance in him; who also conspicuously fought wild beasts. For when the proconsul was wishing to persuade him and was saying to have pity on his age, he dragged the wild beast to himself, forcing it, wishing to be released more quickly from their unjust and lawless life. From this, therefore, all the crowd, having marveled at the nobility of the God-loving and God-fearing race of the Christians, shouted: Away with the atheists; let Polycarp be sought.

choices.why: The superlative of γενναῖος conveys both courage and high character; 'most noble' preserves the moral elevation the crowd later marvels at.
The verb means to impart strength or courage; the object 'cowardice' is paradoxical and must be kept literal to show he was fortifying what was weak in them.
The compound verb means to fight against beasts in the arena; a literal rendering keeps the technical sense of the martyrdom context.

choices.english: to have pity on his youth
choices.why: ἡλικία here means his age or youthful prime; the infinitive clause is the content of the proconsul's urging, so 'to have pity on his youth' keeps the indirect speech clear.
rejected: to take pity on his young age

choices.why: The aorist middle participle means compelling or forcing the beast toward himself; 'forcing it' keeps the active, deliberate agency of Germanicus.
The imperative αἶρε means 'take away' or 'remove'; 'Away with' is the standard English idiom for a crowd's demand to eliminate someone, and 'atheists' follows the glossary for ἄθεοι.

pass_b_english: But thanks be to God, for the enemy did not prevail against them all. The most noble Germanicus encouraged the others by his endurance, and he fought the wild beasts with distinction. When the proconsul tried to persuade him and told him to have pity on his youth, Germanicus dragged the beast toward himself, forcing it on, because he wanted to be released quickly from their unjust and lawless life.
At this the whole crowd marveled at the nobility of the God-loving and God-fearing race of the Christians, and they shouted, "Away with the atheists! Find Polycarp!"

problems.why: ἐπερρώννυεν here means 'emboldened/encouraged' their cowardice—i.e., overcame it, not 'strengthened' it as a quality; the sense is he rallied them out of cowardice.
ἡλικία means 'age' (here old age, given context of pity), not 'youth'; Germanicus is portrayed as elderly.

problems.quote: the devil did not prevail against any of them
problems.why: Source says 'he/it did not prevail against all of them'—no 'devil' is named; subject is unstated, likely the persecutors' efforts or Satan implicitly, but adding 'the devil' is an interpretive addition not in the Greek.
problems.fix: for he did not prevail against any of them
problems.ruling: No 'devil' in κατὰ πάντων γὰρ οὐκ ἴσχυσεν; unstated subject added interpretively, changing meaning.

edits.old: But thanks be to God, for the devil did not prevail against any of them.
edits.new: But thanks be to God, for he did not prevail against any of them.

edits.old: The most noble Germanicus was strengthening their cowardice through his own endurance
edits.new: The most noble Germanicus was emboldening them against their cowardice through his own endurance

edits.old: told him to have pity on his youth
edits.new: told him to have pity on his age

fixed: Changed 'the devil did not prevail' to 'he did not prevail' since the Greek does not name the devil.
Changed 'strengthening their cowardice' to 'emboldening them against their cowardice' to reflect the sense of overcoming cowardice.
Changed 'his youth' to 'his age' since the Greek refers to age, not youth.

problems.quote: he did not prevail against any of them
problems.why: Subject is wrong: 'he' should be 'it' (the devil/evil one implied from context), and 'any' flips to 'all'.
problems.fix: for it did not prevail against them all
problems.ruling: κατὰ πάντων means 'against all'; 'any' flips meaning. Subject is contextually the devil/evil one, not 'he' (God).

edits.old: But thanks be to God, for he did not prevail against any of them.
edits.new: But thanks be to God, for it did not prevail against them all.

fixed: The other reported problems were not real; the English already matched the source.

problems.quote: he wanted to be released quickly from their unjust and lawless life
problems.why: 'Their' seems to refer to persecutors' life, but Germanicus wants release from his own life.
problems.fix: Emend to 'this' or 'the' unjust and lawless life.

edits.old: he wanted to be released quickly from their unjust and lawless life
edits.new: he wanted to be released quickly from this unjust and lawless life

fixed: The other previously tried edits are not reflected in the current English, so no further changes are needed.

problems.quote: Germanicus strengthened the others in their fear through his own endurance, and he fought the wild beasts with distinction.
problems.why: The sentence contradicts itself—‘strengthened… in their fear’ is incoherent.
problems.fix: Rewrite: “Germanicus encouraged the others by his courage and fought the beasts bravely.”

edits.old: The most noble Germanicus strengthened the others in their fear through his own endurance, and he fought the wild beasts with distinction.
edits.new: The most noble Germanicus encouraged the others by his courage and fought the wild beasts bravely.

last_rejected.quote: Germanicus was emboldening them against their cowardice
last_rejected.source_quote: ὁ γὰρ γενναιότατος Γερμανικὸς ἐπερρώννυεν αὐτῶν τὴν δειλίαν διὰ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ ὑπομονῆς
last_rejected.why: Germanicus emboldened their cowardice, not emboldened them against their cowardice; he strengthened the cowardice itself by example.
last_rejected.fix: Germanicus was strengthening their cowardice through his endurance in him
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπερρώννυεν αὐτῶν τὴν δειλίαν: he strengthened/emboldened them against their cowardice; English captures sense adequately.

last_rejected.quote: because he wanted to be released quickly from their unjust and lawless life
last_rejected.source_quote: βουλόμενος τάχιον τοῦ ἀδίκου καὶ ἀνόμου βίου αὐτῶν ἀπαλλαγῆναι
last_rejected.why: αὐτῶν refers to the crowd/pagans, not Germanicus; he wanted to escape from their life, not be released from his own.
last_rejected.fix: wanting to be freed more quickly from their unjust and lawless life
last_rejected.ruling: αὐτῶν refers to pagans/crowd; English 'their unjust and lawless life' correctly attributes life to them, not Germanicus.

polish.changed: Clarified that Germanicus strengthened the other martyrs, made the proconsul's persuasion explicit, identified the crowd as the speakers, and smoothed the sentence flow for reading aloud.
Clarified that Germanicus encouraged the others by his endurance rather than in their fear, and identified him as a martyr who fought the wild beasts.

notes.why: No identification of who Germanicus is.
notes.fix: Add a brief note (e.g., “Germanicus, a Christian martyr mentioned in the letter”).

notes.quote: Germanicus strengthened the others in their fear through his own endurance, and he fought the wild beasts with distinction.
notes.why: The sentence contradicts itself—‘strengthened… in their fear’ is incoherent.
notes.fix: Rewrite: “Germanicus encouraged the others by his courage and fought the beasts bravely.”
